# Transparency for a Workload-Adaptive Cognitive Agent in a Manned–Unmanned Teaming Application

Gunar Roth , Axel Schulte, Fabian Schmitt, and Yannick Brand

**Abstract—This study focuses on the transparent design of a cognitive agent to enhance situation awareness in two aspects of a human-agent teaming application: assisted system management and mixed-initiative mission planning. Adaptive and complex agent behavior might result in the failure to comprehend resulting interventions, a decrease in trust, and a loss of overall situation awareness. This study describes and validates a concept for transparent agent design by adopting the transparency strategies proposed by the “situation awareness-based agent transparency model.” The overall objective was to improve the human operator’s perception, comprehension, and projection of the agent’s support. The concept was applied to the prototype of a workload-adaptive cognitive agent, which supports a helicopter crew during mission planning and execution in complex and dynamically changing multi-vehicle missions. A human-in-the-loop experiment revealed enhancements in situation awareness and performance. Subjective trust measures implied an increase in human-like characteristics of the cognitive agent. The results and the potential for further research are discussed.**

**Index Terms—Adaptive associate systems, cognitive agents, human factors, human-agent teaming, scalable autonomy, situation awareness (SA), transparency.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

HE future of human-machine scenarios is highly affected by the continuous advances in hardware and software technology. The benefits of improved accuracy and speed lead to tasks being increasingly assigned to machines instead of humans. However, some tasks will remain so important that they demand human’s final decision authority. The scenario of multi-ple humans manually controlling simple machines consequently shifts to a few operators with supervisory control tasks over highly complex systems [1].

The processing of large amounts of dynamically changing information under time pressure might result in a significant increase in operator taskload and multitasking demands. To mitigate human error and reduce the risk of excessive taskload without increasing the manpower, it is necessary to support the human operator performing supervisory control tasks. A workload-adaptive cognitive agent can balance mental workload (MWL) and associated human error by temporarily undertaking taskload from the operator [2]. Possible drawbacks might be difficulties to sustain a sufficient and stable mental model of the cognitive agent’s behavior, which can result in a loss of situation awareness (SA) and degraded trust in the agent.

Within this paper, we address the enhancement of operator SA by increasing the transparency of a cognitive agent, which supports vehicle control and mission planning.

## II. APPLICATION

Our research comprises the teaming of manned and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in dynamic and complex military missions. Thereby, a single manned two-seated helicopter is responsible for the command and control of multiple UAVs according to a task-based guidance approach [3]. The unmanned vehicles serve as detached sensor platforms in order to increase the sensor range of the helicopter. The pilot-flying is responsible for the basic flying tasks and the management of the helicopter’s subsystems (e.g., navigation, communication, etc.). The pilotin-command, in the following called “operator,” is fully responsible for the tactical planning and re-planning of the manned helicopter as well as the unmanned vehicles during the mission. Mission planning tasks include helicopter route planning, contingency planning, and UAV task planning. Both the pilot and the operator use multi-functional displays in the helicopter cockpit to perform their individual tasks. Whereas the operator uses a tactical map display to sketch routes and command tasks to the unmanned systems, the pilot-flying utilizes the displays to monitor and adjust the helicopter’s systems.

Due to highly demanding tasks in complex scenarios, critical mission situations may result in a significant increase in the pilot’s and the operator’s MWL. This potentially results in performance decrease and human error.

Our approach comprises a workload-adaptive cognitive agent, which supports each crew member individually and uses dynamically varying levels of assistance. It automatically adjusts this level depending on the current MWL-states of the individual crew members and the criticality of the environmental (e.g., tactical) situation. The MWL estimate is based on an activity determination and an online taskload assessment [4]. The taskload is calculated according to a task model with individual demands based on the “Multiple Resource Theory” [5]. The agent’s support includes attention guidance, task simplification, and task adoption [2]. However, as long as the pilot and the operator are performing well at moderate workload and no assistance is required, the agent remains silent. Moreover, the crew members have final decision authority and are always enabled to override the agent’s actions. Fig. 1 schematically displays the structure of our application in the work-system notation<sup>1</sup> of [6]. The operator, the pilot, and the agent are depicted on the left side in Fig. 1.

The agent was integrated into a research helicopter mission simulator, which was established for studying the joint missionaccomplishment in manned–unmanned teaming scenarios.

## A. Support on Mission Planning

The agent assists the operator based on the concept of the scalable mixed initiative. It supports the task assignments to the UAVs as well as the route planning of both the helicopter and the UAVs. Furthermore, it is enabled to identify plan conflicts and optimize the mission plan. Thereby, the agent can assist in two different levels of automation: low- and high-automated mission planning [7].

The low-automated mission planning shall encourage the operator to plan on his or her own by just proposing particular steps in the mission planning and allowing the operator enough time to understand the proposal, re-engage the planning process, and continue the planning without the agent’s support. Its purpose is to guide attention to a problem in the mission plan and help the operator get back into the mission planning after being diverted by other tasks.

The high-automated mission planning support is more of a backup tool in case of an emergency. This function provides an extensive plan proposal to the operator in critical situations where manual planning was either completely skipped or at least associated with high costs or risks. Such situations could be a lengthy delay when being threatened by a hostile force. In these cases, the planning agent tries to prevent further harm by suggesting multiple tasks at once and thereby simplifying the situation. Such proposals are more complex and designed to solve a critical situation rapidly. However, they increase the likelihood that the operator’s SA is reduced. To counteract this, the operator needs explanatory information and sufficient time to make an accurate decision about it.

## B. Support on System Management

Additionally, the agent supports the pilot-flying during mission execution by identifying and guiding attention on neglected system management tasks, as for instance the setup of flight phase configurations or the transponder settings. It is able to project future situations with high MWL demands that can cause SA and performance decrements. Using this knowledge, the agent balances predicted workload peaks by proactively simplifying the up-coming tasks. Finally, the agent is enabled to intervene and adopt system management tasks in order to pre-vent human error, which could result in harm for the helicopter’s crew [8].

The agent interacts with the pilot and the operator dialogbased using either text boxes on the multi-functional displays or voice interactions.

Even though increasing the agent’s level of automation should have beneficial effects on the MWL [9], an accompanied drawback might be diminished SA. Due to the agent’s adaptive intervention strategy and complex reasoning, the crew members may experience difficulties understanding the agent’s decisions and actions. A good balance of SA and MWL is especially important in situations with high mental demand. Transparent behavior is, therefore, an essential factor in the application of a workloadadaptive cognitive agent. More information on our application can be found in [10].

## III. CONCEPT FOR INCREASED TRANSPARENCY

In order to acquire high performance in human-agent teams, it is crucial that the agent’s actions, reasoning process, and pre-dicted outcomes are comprehensible to the operator and the pilot. Without this understanding, two main human performance issues may result: a loss of SA and a decrease in trust. The SA-based agent transparency (SAT) model [11] addresses these problems by identifying transparency requirements in order to understand task parameters, logic, and predicted outcomes of an intelligent agent in a human-agent team. Our approach to enhance the crew’s awareness of the agent’s interventions was applying the strategies proposed by this model and increasing the agent’s transparency. This model proposes to provide agent information in three levels according to Endsley’s levels of SA [11] [12]:

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>1</sup>The work system notation is a depiction of the physical dimensions of all entities involved in the work process of a human-machine system. The humanmachine system is differentiated into the workers on the left-hand side and the tools on the right hand side. Workers comprise all members those are controlling the work process by the use of the tools provided to them. A worker has knowledge of the work objective, tries to achieve it by own initiative and is also allowed to change the work objective by own will. Furthermore, the impact of environmental conditions, supply, and information is affecting the worker’s behavior and decision-making. In order to achieve the work objective, the worker uses tools, which function as subordinates in a hierarchically degraded relation to the worker. They can be categorized in three groups: worksite settings, non-powered tools, and powered tools. The worker’s choice and use of the tools will consecutively result in the output of the work system. A work system must contain at least one human worker in order to be defined as a human machine system, but not necessarily all workers need to be of human nature (e.g., the cognitive agent worker shown in Fig. 1).</span></small>

**SAT L1:** Enhancing the perception of the agent’s actions by answering the question “What is going on and what is the agent trying to achieve?”

**SAT L2:** Improving the comprehension of the agent’s behavior by answering the question “Why does the agent do $i t _ { \cdot } ^ { \mathrm { ~ \scriptsize ~ \prime ~ \prime ~ } }$

**SAT L3:** Enhancing the projection of the agent’s outcomes by answering the question “What should the operator expect to happen?”

Derived from this model, our general approach consisted of the following rules: On SAT L1, the agent shall provide information about ongoing interventions and its current intention. To enhance the comprehension aspect of the agent’s behavior on SAT L2, the agent shall convey the information about why it decided to intervene in a specific manner. On SAT L3, the human shall be provided with projection information about the agent’s state and behavior in the near future as well as the agent’s prediction of future states.

Due to the different responsibilities of the operator and the pilot in the manned–unmanned teaming scenario, our concept to enhance the agent’s transparency involved two concepts, one for each crew member.

## IV. IMPLEMENTATION

## A. Mission Planning

Concerning the mission planning, the first transparency level describes what information should be displayed to support the operator in perceiving the agent’s current planning proposals and the general settings in which the agent’s planning process is based on. Settings comprise, for example, whether the agent is supposed to propose planning steps for the helicopter, the UAVs, or both. This level excludes all information about the planner’s reasoning and all information associated with temporal information. We implemented a status display on the tactical map, which contains the agent’s planning-goal and current level of automation to the operator (see bottom left in Fig. 2). The LOA slider indicates the agent’s current level of automation with the options “off” (left), “low” (middle), and “high” (right) and serves as a tool to acknowledge the agent’s current level of automation. The buttons represent the agent’s permissions and are marked with a green indicator when activated. In our application, the agent was allowed to propose missing HC Tasks (“Append HC”) and missing UAV Tasks (“Append UAV”). The remaining buttons would have allowed the agent to propose an alternative HC route (“Alt. HC Route”), alternative UAV routes (“Alt. UAV Route”), or to suggest switching tasks assigned to a single UAV (“Reassign single UAV”) or between multiple UAVs (“Reassign multi UAV”) if it was beneficial to the mission plan. Along with the implemented plan, the status display indicates the parameters that were the basis of the agent’s planning proposals. The menu primarily serves as a utility to display the agent’s settings so that the operator can crosscheck them. It could also be implemented to provide the operator the means to adjust the parameters, adding an adaptable feature to the automation. As soon as a (partial) mission plan exists, the spatial information of this plan is visualized on the tactical map as an overlay on top of the surrounding geographical properties, infrastructure, and tactical situation. The planned tasks and their corresponding routes are displayed in the color of the respective vehicle along its designated way. They are either visualized as solid lines in case of the helicopter or as arrows in case of the UAVs. An alternative helicopter route is displayed as a dashed line. Instead of a text, symbols next to routes represent the associated tasks to decrease clutter. An overview of the symbols and their corresponding tasks is displayed in Table I.

Routes and tasks proposed by the agent are visualized similar to the already implemented plan. Proposals to add missing tasks will be displayed as a continuation of the plan and proposals to adjust the plan will just outline the parts that should be adapted. The proposals are highlighted in purple to attract the operator’s attention. Additionally to the visualization in the map, proposed tasks are communicated through a dialog box when a re-planning event occurs (see top of Fig. 2).

TABLE II IMPLEMENTED REASON SYMBOLS

| Symbol | Description |
| --- | --- |
|  | Task Missing:The proposed task is essential to the mission planning and absent in the currently implemented plan. |
|  | Optimization:The proposal optimizes the currently implemented plan regarding associated costs. |
|  | Goal changed:Re-planning due to a change of the mission goal (e.g. changed landing-point). |
|  | Threat:The proposal suggests circumventing a possible hazard that threatens parts of the mission plan. |
|  | Added capabilities:The UAV tasks can be reassigned due to an increased number of available UAVs. |
|  | Capabilities lost:The UAV tasks need to be reassigned due to a decreased number of available UAVs. |

The second transparency level serves to provide the operator information about the connection between the input and the output of the agent, i.e., help the operator to understand the agent’s reasoning to propose a specific planning step. Information on the agent’s reasoning was presented in the agent’s plan to the operator. The reasons (e.g., a change in the tactical situation) that necessitated the agent to intervene and adapt the mission plan were conveyed by pictorial symbols to decrease clutter in the tactical map. Table II gives an overview of the implemented reason symbols and their meaning.

The third transparency level aims to support the operator by projecting the future vehicle states (like position and task progress) and the future mission state. The agent’s projection of the mission plan includes spatial and temporal information. The spatial information was already illustrated as routes on the tactical map display in the previous transparency level. Thus, projective time information still needed to be provided to the operator. For each implemented task, the agent generates a tasksequence for the helicopter and each of the UAVs. Based on the vehicles’ velocities and the expected timespan to accomplish individual jobs, the agent continuously calculates the expected start times, durations, and end times for each task. To make this information more transparent to the operator, a detached timeline was developed (see right side of Fig. 2). It provides the temporal information of the implemented plan and the proposals that serve to augment the spatial information.

To summarize, information was implemented at the following SAT levels [13]:

**Level 1:** The agent’s goal, settings, and level of automation.

**Level 2:** Symbols representing the events that justified an intervention.

## B. System Management

To support the first transparency level of the system management, we implemented a retrospective listing of all the tasks that the agent already adopted (“Adopted Tasks” in Fig. 3). The provision of the current and previous interventions is supposed to convey the present task situation and prevent double execution.

On the second transparency level, the agent communicates its decision parameters for specific interventions. Factors of influence in the decision process are critical events, neglected tasks, and the pilot’s estimated workload. Three elements were implemented to provide these triggers to the pilot. Once the agent detects a critical event that affects the mission conduction (e.g., low oil pressure), it is displayed to the pilot as long as it is influencing the agent’s decision process (“Critical Events” in Fig. 3). A listing of the neglected system management tasks informs the pilot about the critical divergences between necessary and already performed tasks, which required the agent to intervene (“Neglected Tasks” in Fig. 3). The agent’s estimate of the pilot’s current workload represents the final essential decision parameter and is visualized on a clock instrument (“Current Load” in Fig. 3). It essentially influences the agent’s intervention strategy concerning type and time of action. During high estimated workload phases, the agent intervenes faster and to a greater extent in order to reduce the pilot’s taskload and subsequent MWL.

The third transparency level addresses the agent’s future level of assistance and the predicted time that the agent will start to support the human. By listing all outstanding tasks and their associated priority (“To Do Tasks” in Fig. 3), the agent pre-announces upcoming interventions. In addition, the predicted future workload of the pilot was displayed in a separate column of the already mentioned timeline to show predictions of upcoming workload peaks and increased agent assistance (right in Fig. 3).

To summarize, information was implemented at the following SAT levels:

**Level 1:** “Adopted Tasks”-list.

**Level 2:** “Critical Events”-list, “Neglected Tasks”-list, and “Current Load”-indicator.

**Level 3:** “To Do Tasks”-list and a timeline presenting the pre-dicted future workload.

The implemented display elements, besides addressing the different SAT levels, had distinct temporal features [14].

1) Prospective announcement of intended intervention prior to any assistance.

2) Notification about present intervention.

3) Retrospective report of performed tasks after the intervention.

## V. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION

In order to evaluate the proposed agent transparency design, we developed a human-in-the-loop simulation experiment, whereby each participant consecutively adopted the roles of the operator and the pilot-flying in a manned–unmanned teaming configuration. With the aid of three UAVs, the participants had to plan and subsequently perform a helicopter transport mission including takeoff, transit, and landing.

## A. Hypotheses

The following hypotheses were derived from the SAT model. By providing the additional transparency elements, we expected the following.

1) Participants will exhibit higher SA when the agent provides them with information at a higher level of transparency.

2) Participants will exhibit higher trust in the agent when it provides them with information at a higher level of transparency.

3) The human-agent team will perform better (lower error rate, faster response times) on achieving the mission goals when the agent’s behavior is more transparent due to a higher level of transparency.

4) Participants will report differences in their MWL between conditions that had a low level of transparency compared to those with a high level of transparency.

## B. Procedure

The participants received a 90-min training prior to the start of the experiment to familiarize them with the system and the agent. A presentation included information about the general structure of the experiment, a context for the missions, their tasks, and how the agent would support them during the missions. Furthermore, the presentation elucidated the functional design, structure, and control of the system, in particular the two different designs (low and high transparent) used in the experiment. This included the relevant elements in the map as well as the appearance and handling of the agent’s interventions in the design with less transparency information. Furthermore, the additional elements in the design, which provided more transparency information, like the timeline, were explained. At the end of the training, the participants were asked to perform practice exercises, which included picture- and video-based training.

The experiment consisted of two missions, which were again separated into two parts: mission planning and subsequently system management. Our research generally requires an operator and pilot-flying to perform mission planning and system management concurrently. However, in order to avoid interferences across subjects, we separated those tasks so the experiment was manageable by a single participant.

In the first part, the participants took on the role of the operator and planned the mission in cooperation with the agent. Thereby, the subjects had to decide about the validity of the agent’s proposals and find violations of previously given constraints. The mission planning part initially started with planning proposals on the low level of automation, meaning multiple individual steps separated by a time delay. Following the initial planning, a change of the tactical situation required an immediate reaction. To simplify the situation, the agent increased its assistance to the high level of automation and generated an extensive replanning proposal that combined multiple planning steps for the helicopter and the UAVs.

After the planning, the participants took on the role of the pilot-flying and conducted the mission. During this phase, their task was to monitor the system management interface during the mission progress and to perceive and comprehend the agent’s assistance. Flight control tasks were not part of the experiment and were instead automatically performed. Halfway through the system management, participants were tasked to additionally solve a basic math task every 20 s. The accompanied higher demand of mental resources simulated the cause for a subsequent workload-triggered increase of agent’s assistance.

The main difference between the two missions was the level of transparency displayed to the participant. The participants were confronted with all transparency elements within one mission, whereas the other mission served as a low transparent reference value. However, the additional transparency elements in the high transparent design were not essential to complete the individual tasks. Instead, they served to improve SA and support accurate decision-making. Otherwise, the missions were similar in terms of context, length, complexity, and difficulty of the task. Each mission lasted for approximately 35 min.

## C. Experimental Design

The participant’s workplace consisted of one monitor showing either the display of Fig. 2 during the mission planning or the display visualized in Fig. 3 during the system management. The start and pause of the experiment as well as the changes in the tactical situation were triggered by the experimenters from a nearby control station.

The participants consisted of two female and eight male students between 19 and 30 years of age (M = 24.5, SD = 3.5) majoring at the University of Central Florida.

Due to the small group of available subjects, we abstained from a control group and chose a within-subjects design, whereby each participant was asked to complete all experimental conditions.

The participants observed eight different conditions of the agent, which varied from low $( A _ { \mathrm { L o } } )$ to high assistance $( A _ { \mathrm { H i } } )$ and less $( T _ { \mathrm { L o } } )$ to more displayed transparency information $( T _ { \mathrm { H i } } )$ Moreover, the conditions were separated concerning the tasks the participants had to perform: mission planning (p) and system management (m). We distributed the conditions equally on the two missions. The conditions and their order in the low transparent design were:

$( \mathbf { T _ { L o } A _ { L o } } ) _ { \mathbf { p } }$ low transparent design (only SAT L1 information) and low level of automation;

$( \bf { T } _ { L o } \bf { A } _ { H i } ) _ { p }$ low transparent design and high level of automation;

$( \mathbf { T _ { L o } A _ { L o } } ) _ { \mathbf { m } }$ low transparent design (only notifications about present interventions) and low level of automation;

$( \mathbf { T _ { L o } A _ { H i } } ) _ { \mathbf { m } }$ low transparent design and high level of automation.

The conditions and their order in the high transparent design were:

$( \mathbf { T _ { H i } A _ { L o } } ) _ { \mathbf { p } }$ high transparent design (SAT L1+2+3 information) and low level of automation;

$( \bf { T } _ { H i } \bf { A } _ { H i } ) _ { p }$ high transparent design and high level of automation;

$( \mathbf { T _ { H i } A _ { L o } } ) _ { \mathbf { m } }$ high transparent design (SAT L1+2+3 information) and low level of automation;

$( \bf { T } _ { H i } \bf { A } _ { H i } ) _ { m }$ high transparent design and high level of automation.

In order to counterbalance carry-over-effects accompanied by our experimental design, we randomized the order of the conditions. However, randomization was limited to the extent of transparency due to logical mission constraints. Half of the population received the low transparent design in the first mission, followed by the high transparent design in the second mission, and the other half vice versa.

Using a repeated measures data collection method, we assessed the dependent measures SA, trust, and perceived workload. Thereby, the participants had to answer multiple questionnaires prior, during, and after each mission. Participants’ SA was assessed with a freeze probe situation recall that was aligned to assess SA at each of the three levels [15] and the situational awareness rating technique (SART) [16]. We used the Trust between People and Automation questionnaire [17] as well as the Godspeed questionnaire [18] to acquire trust measures. The participants self-reported their perceived MWL according to a Bedford mental workload scale [19]. During the mission planning, we also recorded the response times and accuracy of the decisions in order to acquire performance measures. To analyze the dependent measures, we completed a series of paired t-tests.

## VI. RESULTS

## A. Situation Awareness

SA probe scores improved as a function of increase in SAT levels in all conditions. We observed higher SA in the lower $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 1 . 6 1 7 ;   \mathtt { p } = 0 . 0 0 8 )$ and higher automated mission planning $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 1 . 4 6 3 ; \; \mathrm { p }   =   0 . 0 0 8 )$ as well as during the lower $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 2 . 7 0 4 ; \mathtt { p } < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ and higher automated $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 1 . 9 6 8 ;$ $\mathtt { p } = 0 . 0 0 2 )$ system management task, as shown in Fig. 4.

A comparison of the particular scores in the SA measure indicated that the subjects’ SA increased most in the projection level, the highest SA level. The SART measure showed no significant change in the participant’s overall SA. However, a previous study found the SART to be unaffected in terms of changes in interface designs [20].

## B. Performance

Performance was only evaluated in the mission planning phase. We assessed participants’ time and accuracy in responding to the agent’s interventions (see Figs. 5 and 6, respectively). Approximately 20% of the agent’s proposals during the experiment violated at least one of the given constraints and had to be declined. Correct decisions were the approval of correct proposals and the disapproval of incorrect proposals. Consequently, the disapproval of correct and the approval of incorrect proposals were counted as wrong.

The time required to determine the validity of a planning proposal was significantly reduced by providing additional transparency information in both the low $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } =   0 . 5 2 9 ;$

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 6. Accuracy results.

$\mathtt { p } = 0 . 0 0 3 )$ and the high automated mission planning $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } =$ $0 . 4 2 2 ; \mathtt { p } = 0 . 0 3 6 )$ . Although the interface contained more data to process, we conclude that the participants’ decision process was expedited by the additional transparency information. The verification of constraints concerning the temporal impact of proposals can especially be accomplished much faster since necessary SA information on levels 2 and 3 was provided. Moreover, the response times in the high-automated mission planning appear generally higher than in the low-automated mission planning. We ascribe this to the higher complexity of the extensive proposals on the higher level of automation. They consisted of multiple task proposals, partially for different vehicles, which had to be taken into account individually before deciding about the overall approval.

The subjects’ ability to approve correct and disapprove incorrect planning proposals revealed a mentionable but non-significant enhancement when additional transparency information was provided. We consequently conclude that the accuracy remained constant. According to the speed–accuracy tradeoff, faster response times and constant accuracy imply increased performance. We, therefore, conclude that the performance increased in both mission planning parts due to the higher transparency.

## C. Trust

Subjective trust measures with the Trust between People and Automation and the Godspeed questionnaires showed inconclusive results. Within the mission planning phase, higher transparency showed no significant effect on the participants trust in the agent according to the Trust between People and Automation questionnaire [see Fig. 7(a)]. However, there was a NS $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 0 . 2 5 ; \mathtt { p } = 0 . 0 8 6 )$ trend toward improved trust as a function of higher levels of SAT for the system management task [see Fig. 7(b)]. Moreover, the participants perceived the agent to be more humanlike. The characteristics of anthropomorphism $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 0 . 4 8 ;   \mathrm { p }   =   0 . 0 2 6 )$ , perceived intelligence $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 0 . 6 5 ;$ $\mathtt { p } = 0 . 0 1 3 )$ , and animacy $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 0 . 4 6 ;   \mathrm { p } = 0 . 0 4 9 )$ increased.

In contrast, the high transparent agent was attributed a lower anthropomorphism $( d _ { \mathrm { a v } } = 0 . 6 5 5 , \; \mathrm { p }   =   0 . 0 1 4 )$ in the mission planning. These results correlate with findings in a different study [21].

One explanation for these inconclusive results is how the transparency information was communicated in the present experiment. Information concerning planning was more abstract in comparison to information pertaining to system management. Abstract communication might, therefore, be perceived as machine-like behavior, which is again linked to decreased trust in the agent.

## D. Workload

During the mission planning, the participants reported no differences in their MWL. On average, the subjects reported low MWL in all four conditions of the mission planning [see Fig. 8(a)]. We had assumed that the participants would experience an increase in MWL due to the perception of additional information. However, we conclude that this was compensated by the information’s content, which saved mental resources to establish SA. The assessment during the system management revealed a significant workload increase between the low- and high-taskload phase $( ( T _ { \mathrm { L o } } A _ { \mathrm { L o } } ) _ { m }$ vs. $( T _ { \mathrm { L o } } A _ { \mathrm { H i } } ) _ { m }$ and $( T _ { \mathrm { H i } } A _ { \mathrm { L o } } ) _ { m }$ vs. $( T _ { \mathrm { H i } } A _ { \mathrm { H i } } ) _ { m } )$ in Fig. 8(b). We conclude this resulted from the additional math tasks, which were intentionally introduced to simulate a high workload situation. In addition, the subjects gave a slightly higher workload rating in the high transparency conditions $( ( T _ { \mathrm { L o } } A _ { \mathrm { L o } } ) _ { m }$ vs. $( T _ { \mathrm { H i } } A _ { \mathrm { L o } } ) _ { m }$ and $( T _ { \mathrm { L o } } A _ { \mathrm { H i } } ) _ { m }$ vs. $( T _ { \mathrm { H i } } A _ { \mathrm { H i } } ) _ { m } )$ in Fig. 8(b). This might be caused by the additional transparency information communicated by the agent, which had to be perceived by the subjects.

## E. Comments Made by the Participants

In a feedback survey, the participants reported that they found the timeline and the “To Do Tasks” list most helpful. Interestingly, this rating correlates with the third SAT-level, supporting the projection of the agent’s outcomes. Since the projection is the highest level of SA, it requires the most effort to be acquired. Accordingly, the support on this level reduces mental resources and is, therefore, likely to be seen as more helpful.

## VII. CONCLUSION

Our study investigated the effects of providing additional agent information to the human member in a human–agent team. In order to increase SA in a manned–unmanned teaming configuration, our approach consisted of increasing agent transparency. Our concept to identify and classify important agent information was based on the SAT-model. We accordingly developed interface elements and implemented them into the prototype of a workload adaptive cognitive agent. A human-in-the-loop experiment was designed to investigate the impact of increased transparency in two applications: mission planning and system management. Besides the effect on SA, we additionally investigated the influences on trust in automation, task performance, and MWL.

An evaluation of our SA assessment showed significant in creases on all three levels with the provision of additional transparency elements. We observed the highest increase in the projection level. We, therefore, infer that higher agent transparency improved the general perception, comprehension, and particularly the projection of the agent’s interventions.

A performance measure in the mission planning task revealed that the subjects responded faster when provided with additional transparency information on a higher transparency level. Accuracy measures showed no considerable impact concerning the participants’ correct usage of the agent as a result from a higher transparency level. However, the combination of improved response times and constant accuracy still indicates a higher performance due to the additional transparency information.

Subjective trust measures implied that the participants’ trust in the agent partially improved. Whereas the enhancement was observed during the system management, no effect was noticeable in the mission planning.

A subjective MWL rating implied no changes in participants workload during the mission planning and a workload increase in the system management task. However, we assume that a workload improvement due to higher transparency has compensated for increased workload in the perception and comprehension of additional information.

In order to comply with time restrictions, it was not possible to run the number of participants that were determined with an a priori power analysis. Trust and accuracy measures showed small effects that could not be verified with statistical significance. A follow-on experiment with a larger and more sophisticated population could investigate these effects and improve the generality of the experiment. Moreover, just two of the possible variations of the level of transparency were tested in order to reduce complexity and expenditure of time. The investigation of more transparency levels could detect particular influences of the different SAT levels on the dependent variables.

The implementation of transparency information on the basis of the SAT model is by no means complete. Especially the levels 2 and 3 still offer the potential to enhance the comprehension and projection of the agent’s actions. Specific properties of proposed routes would, for example, convey the agent’s reasoning process. Moreover, the announcement of upcoming agent interventions concerning the mission planning would fall into the projection level. Future efforts will include integrating transparency into the workload estimate.

To establish SA, humans have to spend mental resources. The higher the SA is supposed to be, the more cognitive effort is required. The provision of transparency information to support their SA can spare these resources and reduce their MWL. On the other hand, the perception and comprehension of complex information entail further MWL costs in return. We, therefore, recommend the careful identification of essential information. However, as long as the identification and presentation of transparency information adhere to human factors principles, increasing agent transparency can have beneficial effects on SA and human-agent team performance.
